extracted.intended_audience: federal agency economists and regulatory analysts preparing regulatory impact analyses (and stakeholders commenting on Circular A-4)
extracted.subtask_short: discount rate guidance for regulatory analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, reporting, and updating discount rates and related adjustments (risk, capital, shadow prices) in U.S. federal regulatory cost‑benefit analysis under OMB Circular A-4. Covers frequency/precision of updates, use of multiple rates, treatment of risk, and accounting for capital effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of SRTP updates
rubrics_metrics.description: How often OMB will update the social rate of time preference (SRTP) estimate and associated discount rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB will update the SRTP estimate every three years (next update in 2026) and update Circular A-94’s Appendix D in sync. Three-year updates balance use of recent data against year-to-year instability; less frequent updates would leave underlying data further out of date, while annual updates may impose disproportionate burdens on agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rounding precision for SRTP
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of numeric precision to which the SRTP and recommended rates should be rounded when published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round SRTP to the tenths place. Rounding to tenths provides more accuracy than rounding to whole percentage points and, combined with three-year updates, reduces instability and avoids large spuriously generated changes due solely to rounding (e.g., shifts from 2.49% to 2.51%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of retrospective averaging window
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the retrospective averaging window used to estimate the SRTP (e.g., 30-year average).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a 30-year retrospective average to balance the benefits of incorporating more recent data against year-to-year volatility. OMB concluded a 30-year window appropriately balances recency and stability and illustrated how the 30-year average has changed since 2003.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple discount rates (and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how agencies should present analyses using more than one discount rate to show sensitivity and comparability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular A-4 advises agencies to effectively use three discount/shadow‑price combinations when capital effects are present (see shadow price guidance) rather than multiplying many discount-rate/shadow-price permutations. Presenting the undiscounted annual time stream of impacts (in addition to present values) is the recommended best practice for facilitating sensitivity analysis and calculation of break-even discount rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shadow price of capital approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounting for regulatory effects on capital via a shadow price of capital rather than by using multiple or higher discount rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When regulations are likely to have substantial incidence on capital, apply a closed‑economy shadow price of capital (recommended 1.2). Circular A-4 effectively advises three assumptions for capital effects: (1) discount rate of 2% with shadow price 1 applied to both costs and benefits; (2) 2% with shadow price 1.2 applied to costs; (3) 2% with shadow price 1.2 applied to benefits. Applying a shadow price to benefits or costs is equivalent to using a lower or higher discount rate respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present undiscounted annual time streams
rubrics_metrics.description: Include undiscounted annual streams of costs and benefits alongside present-value calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to present values, agencies should present the undiscounted annual time stream of regulatory impacts; this is the best method to permit sensitivity analysis to any discount rate and to enable calculation of break-even discount rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish risk types when discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and separate at least three ways risk interacts with discounting: yields reflecting risk premia, idiosyncratic risk, and systemic (aggregate) risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Yields used to estimate SRTP may reflect risk premia and thus bias SRTP upward. 2) Idiosyncratic risk (insurable in theory) should be captured via certainty-equivalent valuations unless full insurance is evident. 3) Systemic risk (correlation of regulatory net benefits with aggregate welfare) can in principle be captured via regulation-specific risk premia and betas but requires difficult parameter estimation. Certainty-equivalent valuations should capture both idiosyncratic and systematic risk when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer certainty-equivalent valuation over risk-adjusted discount rates (default)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to adjust discount rates for risk or to adjust monetary values (certainty equivalents) to account for risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general matter, OMB concludes the discount rate should not be adjusted by default to account for uncertainty. Instead, agencies should adjust monetary values of changes in benefits or costs to express them as certainty equivalents. Certainty-equivalent valuations are more flexible and potentially more accurate than applying a single risk‑adjusted discount rate, which assumes exponential growth of uncertainty and can mislead when projects have different risk patterns over time. Agencies may, however, find the risk-adjusted-discount-rate framework conceptually useful in specific contexts and may estimate regulation-specific betas if justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution on using average risk premia or arbitrary betas
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether OMB provides default average systematic risk premia or an average regulatory beta to add to SRTP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB will not advise adding an arbitrary average risk premium to the discount rate because (1) there is no well-developed accepted estimate of regulation-specific betas or average betas across regulations, and (2) many regulations may have negative correlations (insurance value) with aggregate welfare. Use of an arbitrary average could misstate effects and even reverse sign for some regulations. Agencies may estimate regulation-specific betas where evidence supports it, but no default average is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on using market or corporate returns to set social discount rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether private-sector returns (corporate returns, venture capital hurdle rates, investor discount rates) are appropriate bases for the social discount rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use corporate capital returns, venture capital hurdle rates, or private investor discount rates as direct evidence of the risk-free SRTP because such returns may reflect market power, uninternalized externalities, leverage, and other factors not relevant to social valuation. When market evidence is used for risk-premium estimation (e.g., Circular A-94 contexts), leverage adjustments and careful mapping to social outcomes are necessary; commenters’ claims using such private rates do not provide appropriate defaults for SRTP.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to consider longer-term or alternative models (e.g., Ramsey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of alternative models (e.g., Ramsey/CCAPM) for long-term consequences or estimating systematic risk premium endogenously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For regulations where significant consequences extend beyond ~50 years, consideration of a Ramsey model (CCAPM) may be appropriate to handle risk adjustment endogenously. Such approaches can yield very small systematic risk premia (e.g., <0.2% in some calibrations), and different methods yield widely varying estimates; agencies should be cautious and transparent if using such models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat unquantified or poorly measured risk as non‑monetized when certainty-equivalents unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: How to handle risks or biases in SRTP estimates that cannot be reliably quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If certainty-equivalent valuations or well-justified regulation-specific estimates are not available, treat risk (and other uncertain or unquantified factors like behavioral biases, liquidity premia, taxation effects, zero lower bound periods) like other non-monetized regulatory effects rather than adding unsupported default adjustments to the discount rate. OMB emphasizes transparency and that future economic literature progress may enable improved quantification in later revisions.
